label: American Comics
defn: Comic strips and comic books of the United States from the newspaper Sunday pages of the 1890s through the superhero comic book, underground comix and the graphic novel: Winsor McCay's Little Nemo in Slumberland, Herriman's Krazy Kat, Kirby and Lee's Fantastic Four, Spiegelman's Maus.
aliases: US comics;American comic books;American comic strips
see: B1-8 Manga;B1-6 Ligne Claire;B1-7 Marcinelle School;B1-4 Illustration
note: listed after B1-8 Manga with the other comics leaves; 'American comics' is a short Wikipedia page ('Comics of the United States' redirects to American comic book); cartoonists of single-panel gag and editorial cartoons stay in B1-4 Illustration (see kinds)

label: Poster Art
defn: The artistic lithographic poster from the colour posters of Jules Chéret in 1870s Paris through the Belle Époque, the Italian, Swiss and British schools and the psychedelic concert poster: Chéret's Bal du Moulin Rouge, Mucha's Gismonda, Toulouse-Lautrec's Divan Japonais, Cappiello's Le Thermogène.
see: L3 Plakatstil;L4 Soviet Poster;L5 Polish School of Posters;I3-11 Art Nouveau;I3-12 Art Deco
note: 'Poster art' redirects to Poster and 'Affichiste' to Poster artist; Belle Époque poster is unattested as a title, so it is a kind group here, not a leaf

label: Plakatstil
defn: The German 'poster style' founded by Lucian Bernhard's Priester matches poster (1906): a single object, flat colour and a brand name: Bernhard's Priester and Stiller posters, Hohlwein's Riquet, Erdt's Opel, Klinger's Berlin posters.
see: L2 Poster Art

label: Soviet Poster
defn: The political, film and propaganda poster of Soviet Russia and the USSR from 1917 to 1991, from the Civil War lithographs and ROSTA windows through Constructivist photomontage to the TASS windows and Socialist Realist posters: Moor's Have You Volunteered?, Lissitzky's Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge, Stenberg brothers' film posters, Toidze's The Motherland Calls.
aliases: Soviet poster art;Soviet propaganda poster;Russian avant-garde poster
see: L2 Poster Art;A5-63 Constructivism;A5-74 Socialist Realism
note: no Wikipedia article 'Soviet poster' (Propaganda in the Soviet Union is not an art label); attested by The Museum of Russian Art exhibition 'Poster Art of the Soviet Era' and the NMAH TASS-window poster records; ROSTA windows is a Wikipedia-attested kind

label: Polish School of Posters
defn: The Polish poster art of c. 1950–1990 for film, theatre and circus, painterly, metaphorical and hand-lettered, around Henryk Tomaszewski's Warsaw Academy studio: Tomaszewski's Moore, Lenica's Wozzeck, Cieślewicz's Vertigo, Świerzy's Jimi Hendrix.
see: L2 Poster Art;L4 Soviet Poster

label: Treasure Binding
defn: Medieval European book covers worked by goldsmiths in gold, silver-gilt, enamel, gems and carved ivory for Gospel books and altar books, c. 700–1200: Lindau Gospels upper cover, Codex Aureus of St. Emmeram, Ashburnham Pentateuch ivory covers, Gospels of Theodelinda.
aliases: jewelled binding;jeweled book cover;cover of a Gospel book
see: L7 Fine Binding;C3-1 Islamic Bookbinding;G1-43 Mosan Art;D2 Ivory & Bone Carving
note: thin in the object evidence (cover fragments sit under metalwork and ivory); placed as an art-historical form, not a folk craft

label: Fine Binding
defn: Decorated leather bookbinding of Europe and America from the Gothic blind-stamped binding through Renaissance gold tooling to the designer bindings of the 20th century, named after binders, patrons and tooling styles: Grolier bindings, à la fanfare, Le Gascon pointillé, Derome dentelle, Cobden-Sanderson's Doves bindings, Legrain's Art Deco bindings.
aliases: European fine binding;fine bindings;decorated bookbinding;gold-tooled binding
see: C3-1 Islamic Bookbinding;L6 Treasure Binding
note: no Wikipedia 'Fine binding' article; label attested by the Met Watson Library 'Fine Bindings' collection page; ~70 European bindings and binding designs in the Smithsonian evidence

label: Moai
defn: The monolithic statues of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), c. 1250–1500, carved from Rano Raraku tuff and set on ceremonial ahu platforms with red scoria pukao topknots and coral eyes: Ahu Tongariki moai, Hoa Hakananai'a (British Museum), Paro, unfinished moai of Rano Raraku.
aliases: moai statues;Easter Island heads;Rapa Nui stone statues
see: D5-89 Moai Kavakava;K12-5 Marae
note: the ahu platforms stay in K12-5 Marae; the small wooden figures are D5-89; few museum objects (Hoa Hakananai'a, Paris and Brussels heads) but a canonical sculpture tradition

label: Haitian Painting
defn: Painting in Haiti since the founding of the Centre d'Art in Port-au-Prince (1944), from the self-taught masters around DeWitt Peters to the Vodou-inspired Saint-Soleil group (1972) and the Jacmel and Cap-Haïtien schools: Hyppolite's Ogoun Ferraille, Philomé Obin's Funeral of Charlemagne Péralte, Bigaud's Murder in the Jungle, Saint Fleurant's Mother with Children.
see: A5-79 Naïve Art;D5-75 Haitian Metal Art;H4-35 Drapo Vodou
note: Wikipedia 'Haitian painting' redirects to Haitian art#Painting; 17 Haitian painters in artist_placements now in Modern Art or Naïve Art; Tropenmuseum and Smithsonian hold Haitian oils

label: Art Nouveau Glass
defn: Art glass of c. 1885–1915 in Art Nouveau forms and colours: the cameo, acid-etched and marquetry glass of the École de Nancy and the iridescent blown glass of Loetz and of Tiffany: Gallé's Hand with Seaweed and Shells, Daum cameo vases, Loetz Phänomen vases.
aliases: Art Nouveau glass art;École de Nancy glass;art glass
see: L11 Tiffany Glass;I3-11 Art Nouveau;F2 Cut & Carved Glass;F5 Stained Glass
note: cameo glass is carved, so the seam with F2 is by tradition, not technique; leaded windows go to F5

label: Tiffany Glass
defn: The glass of Louis Comfort Tiffany's New York studios (from 1878): iridescent Favrile blown vessels, opalescent glass for leaded lamps and windows, and glass mosaic: Tiffany Favrile vases, Wisteria and Dragonfly lamps, Clara Driscoll's lamp designs.
see: L10 Art Nouveau Glass;F5 Stained Glass;I3-11 Art Nouveau
note: 152 Tiffany and 67 Favrile objects in the Smithsonian evidence; Tiffany windows and lamps also belong to F5 Stained Glass (built by another agent) — keep the windows there and the blown Favrile ware here

label: Studio Glass
defn: The movement of artists making glass in their own studios, begun at Harvey Littleton and Dominick Labino's Toledo workshops (1962) and spread through Pilchuck and the Czech school of cast glass sculpture: Littleton's Arcs, Chihuly's Macchia and Persian series, Libenský and Brychtová's cast sculptures, Tagliapietra's vessels.
aliases: Studio Glass movement;studio art glass;contemporary glass art
see: F1-5 Venetian Glass;I3-16 Contemporary Design;L10 Art Nouveau Glass
note: about 20 studio-glass artists in artist_placements are scattered across painting, photography, sculpture and design leaves

label: Byzantine Enamel
defn: Gold cloisonné enamel of the Byzantine empire, 6th–12th century, in full (Vollschmelz) and sunk (Senkschmelz) techniques, on reliquaries, icons, crowns and book covers: Limburg Staurotheke, Pala d'Oro plaques, Holy Crown of Hungary, Fieschi Morgan Staurotheke.
see: L14 Chinese Cloisonné;L15 Japanese Cloisonné;G1-33 Migration Period Art;A3-2 Byzantine Icons
note: G has no enamel sub-family; placed in G1 by its metal body; few evidence objects but a canonical court art

label: Chinese Cloisonné
defn: Cloisonné enamel on copper and bronze made in China from the early Ming (dated pieces from the Xuande reign, 1426–35) and at its height in the Qing imperial workshops, its turquoise grounds giving the name jingtailan: Xuande-mark lotus jars, Jingtai-mark gu vases, Qianlong cloisonné altar sets and elephants.
see: L15 Japanese Cloisonné;L13 Byzantine Enamel;D3-4 Chinese Snuff Bottles
note: no English Wikipedia article (section Cloisonné#China); Met essay 'Chinese Cloisonné'

label: Japanese Cloisonné
defn: Japanese cloisonné enamel (shippō), revived by Kaji Tsunekichi of Owari in the 1830s and brought to its golden age c. 1880–1910 by the Kyoto and Tokyo workshops, with wired (yūsen) and wireless (musen) pictorial enamels: Namikawa Yasuyuki's Kyoto vases, Namikawa Sōsuke's Akasaka Palace medallions, Andō Jūbei's plique-à-jour.
see: L14 Chinese Cloisonné;L13 Byzantine Enamel;E1-22 Satsuma Ware
note: Wikipedia 'Shippō' redirects to a short 'Shippo' disambiguation page, no enamel article; attested by LACMA and the Ashmolean (Namikawa Yasuyuki gallery); 58 Japanese cloisonné objects in the evidence

label: Quilting
defn: The British and American tradition of pieced (patchwork), appliquéd and whole-cloth quilts from the 18th century, named by pattern, region and type: Baltimore album quilts, Log Cabin and Star of Bethlehem quilts, crazy quilts, Harriet Powers's Bible quilts.
see: H4-46 Amish Quilts;H4-91 Quilts of Gee's Bend;H4-41 Star Quilts;H4-38 Seminole Patchwork;H4-13 Ralli Quilt;H4-42 Tivaevae
note: about 800 quilt and patchwork objects (Smithsonian, world_folk); named community traditions that already have leaves stay separate; label is the field's own umbrella (Wikipedia 'Quilting' and 'History of quilting')

label: African Wax Prints
defn: Roller-printed cotton with a batik-like resin resist made in the Netherlands (Vlisco, from 1846), Britain and later West Africa for West and Central African markets, with named and commemorative designs: Vlisco Dutch wax samples, commemorative portrait cloths, Ankara fancy prints.
see: H5-10 Indonesian Batik;H5-30 Kanga;H5-27 Adire
note: ~190 wax-print objects, mostly Tropenmuseum Vlisco sample books; note H5-30 Kanga carries 'kitenge', the East African name for wax-print cloth — the alias should move here

label: Kimono
defn: The Japanese T-shaped wrapped robe as a dress tradition, from the Momoyama and Edo kosode to the Meiji and modern kimono, with its named garment types and their dyed, woven and embroidered decoration: Edo-period kosode with Ōmi hakkei design, furisode, uchikake wedding robes, katabira summer robes.
see: H5-18 Yūzen;H5-19 Katazome;H5-22 Shibori;H3 Woven Silks & Figured Textiles
note: ~1,400 kimono and kosode objects (ColBase, AIC, Rijksmuseum); P10 bars garment types, but the H7 key admits a dress tradition curated as such, and the field curates kimono as one; the decoration techniques stay in their H5 leaves

label: Queen Anne Style (furniture)
defn: English and American furniture of c. 1700–1755 with cabriole legs, pad and claw-and-ball feet, shell carving and walnut veneers, continuing in the colonies after Queen Anne's reign: Philadelphia and Newport high chests, vase-splat side chairs, bonnet-top highboys.
aliases: Queen Anne furniture;Queen Anne style furniture
see: I3-5 Louis XV Style;L20 Chippendale Furniture;K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture
note: insert in I3 before Chippendale; the architecture of the same name (K2-19) is a 19th-century revival and unrelated

label: Chippendale Furniture
defn: English and American furniture of c. 1750–1790 after Thomas Chippendale's pattern book The Gentleman and Cabinet-Maker's Director (1754), in Rococo, Gothic and Chinese taste in mahogany: Director plates, ribbon-back chairs, Philadelphia Chippendale high chests, Newport block-front desks.
see: L19 Queen Anne Style (furniture);L21 Hepplewhite Style;I3-5 Louis XV Style
note: 'Chippendale furniture' is a Wikipedia redirect to Thomas Chippendale; 42 Director plates in the Smithsonian evidence

label: Hepplewhite Style
defn: English and American Neoclassical furniture of c. 1775–1800 after George Hepplewhite's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Guide (1788): shield- and heart-back chairs, square tapering legs, inlaid satinwood: shield-back chairs, Federal sideboards with spade feet.
see: L22 Sheraton Style;I3-6 Louis XVI Style;L20 Chippendale Furniture
note: 'Hepplewhite style' redirects to George Hepplewhite; Hepplewhite himself now sits in I3-6 Louis XVI Style

label: Sheraton Style
defn: English and American late Neoclassical furniture of c. 1790–1820 after Thomas Sheraton's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Drawing-Book (1791–94): straight lines, turned and reeded legs, painted and inlaid satinwood: Drawing-Book designs, square-back chairs, Duncan Phyfe's early work.
see: L21 Hepplewhite Style;I3-7 Empire Style;I3-6 Louis XVI Style
note: Sheraton himself now sits in I3-6 Louis XVI Style

label: Modernist Photography
defn: The period style of photographers born c. 1860–1944 working in the modern idioms of the 20th century outside a recorded school: sharp-focus, experimental and illustrated-press photography between Pictorialism and the contemporary generation: Stieglitz's The Steerage, Kertész's Fork, Sudek's Prague views.
see: J1-3 Straight Photography;J1-4 New Vision;J1-6 Documentary Photography;J1-7 Contemporary Photography;A5-110 Modern Art
note: period leaf named in P16 but missing from J1; attested as a term by the Met (The Steerage as Stieglitz's 'first modernist photograph'); replaces the current P16 fallback that sends born-1880–1919 photographers to Straight Photography and born-1920–1944 to Documentary Photography (~1,270 low-confidence placements) — re-run P16, not listed one by one

label: Street Photography
defn: Candid photography of chance encounters in public places, mostly with the hand-held camera, from 1930s Paris and New York to the 1960s American and Japanese street: Levitt's children's chalk drawings, Frank's The Americans, Winogrand's Women Are Beautiful, Moriyama's Stray Dog.
see: J1-5 Humanistic Photography;J1-6 Documentary Photography;L25 Photojournalism
note: remove the alias 'street photography' from J1-5 Humanistic Photography; Provoke (Moriyama, Nakahira) is a kind

label: Photojournalism
defn: Photography made to report news for the illustrated press, from the Weimar picture magazines and Life to war and agency photography: Capa's Falling Soldier, Rosenthal's Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima, Eddie Adams's Saigon Execution, Nick Ut's The Terror of War.
see: J1-6 Documentary Photography;L24 Street Photography
note: remove alias 'Photojournalism' from J1-6; Magnum Photos and war photography are kinds

label: Surrealist Photography
defn: Photography of the Surrealist movement and its circles, 1920s–1950s, using rayographs, solarisation, staged mannequins and found street images: Man Ray's Rayographs, Boiffard's Big Toe, Bellmer's La Poupée, Grete Stern's Sueños.
see: A5-66 Surrealism;J1-4 New Vision
note: Wikipedia 'Surrealist photography'; also Met essay 'Photography and Surrealism'; painters who also photographed stay in A5-66

label: Fashion Photography
defn: Photography of clothing and models for fashion magazines and advertising, from de Meyer and Steichen at Vogue to the Avedon–Penn generation and the 1960s London and Paris photographers: Steichen's Art of the Gown (1911), Horst's Mainbocher Corset, Avedon's Dovima with Elephants, Penn's Harlequin Dress.
see: J1-2 Pictorialism;J1-7 Contemporary Photography

label: Düsseldorf School of Photography
defn: The students of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf from 1976, making serial, frontal and large-format colour photographs: the Bechers' Water Towers typologies, Gursky's 99 Cent, Struth's Museum Photographs, Ruff's Portraits.
see: J1-7 Contemporary Photography;A5-34 Düsseldorf School of Painting

label: Persian Garden
defn: The walled garden of Iran laid out as a chahar bagh, four plots divided by water channels around a pavilion, from Achaemenid Pasargadae to the Safavid and Qajar gardens (UNESCO 2011): Pasargadae, Bagh-e Fin, Kashan, Eram Garden, Shiraz, Shazdeh Garden, Mahan.
see: L30 Mughal Garden;K1 Islamic Architecture
note: 'Persian garden' redirects to Persian gardens; Charbagh has its own article (kind)

label: Mughal Garden
defn: The gardens of the Mughal emperors in South Asia, 16th–18th century, built on the chahar bagh with terraces, cascades and tomb or pleasure pavilions: Humayun's Tomb garden, Taj Mahal charbagh, Shalimar Bagh, Srinagar, Shalimar Gardens, Lahore.
see: L29 Persian Garden;K1-15 Mughal Architecture
note: remove the alias 'Mughal gardens' from K1-15 Mughal Architecture

label: Chinese Garden
defn: The Chinese classical garden of rocks, water, pavilions and planting composed as a landscape in miniature, in its imperial and scholar's (literati) forms: Humble Administrator's Garden, Lingering Garden, Summer Palace, Yu Garden.
aliases: Chinese classical garden;scholar's garden;Chinese scholar garden;yuanlin
see: L32 Japanese Garden;A2-3 Literati Painting;K8 East Asian Architecture
note: K8-6 Lingnan Architecture mentions Lingnan gardens; they become a kind here

label: Japanese Garden
defn: The Japanese garden tradition from the Heian pond garden through the Zen dry landscape and the tea garden to the Edo stroll garden: Ryōan-ji rock garden, Saihō-ji moss garden, Katsura Imperial Villa, Kenroku-en.
see: L31 Chinese Garden;K8-12 Shinden-zukuri
note: karesansui and stroll garden are kinds

label: Italian Renaissance Garden
defn: The terraced villa garden of 15th–16th-century Italy, ordered by axis and geometry with fountains, grottoes, statuary and giochi d'acqua: Villa d'Este, Tivoli, Boboli Gardens, Villa Lante, Bagnaia, Sacro Bosco, Bomarzo.
see: L34 French Formal Garden;K5 Early Modern European & Colonial Architecture

label: French Formal Garden
defn: The garden à la française of 17th-century France, a geometric composition of parterres, basins and long axes ordered from the château, perfected by André Le Nôtre: Vaux-le-Vicomte, Gardens of Versailles, Chantilly, Tuileries.
aliases: garden à la française;jardin à la française;French garden;formal garden
see: L33 Italian Renaissance Garden;L35 English Landscape Garden;I3-4 Louis XIV Style

label: English Landscape Garden
defn: The informal 'natural' landscape park of 18th-century Britain, with lawns, serpentine lakes, belts of trees and temples composed as pictures, and its picturesque and international offshoots: Stourhead, Stowe, Blenheim Park, Wörlitz Park.
aliases: English garden;English landscape park;jardin à l'anglaise;landscape garden
see: L34 French Formal Garden;K5 Early Modern European & Colonial Architecture

label: Illusionistic Ceiling Painting
defn: Ceiling and vault painting in fresco that opens the architecture to a painted sky by foreshortening (di sotto in sù) and painted architecture (quadratura), from Mantegna to the Baroque and Rococo: Mantegna's Camera degli Sposi oculus, Pietro da Cortona's Barberini ceiling, Pozzo's Sant'Ignazio, Tiepolo's Würzburg staircase.
aliases: quadratura;di sotto in sù;sotto in su;Baroque ceiling painting
see: L37 Italian Renaissance Fresco;A5-25 Baroque Painting;A5-29 Rococo;L2-44 Gothic Wall Painting
note: 'Quadratura' and 'Di sotto in sù' redirect to sections of this article; specialist quadraturisti move here, history painters who also painted ceilings stay in their A5 leaves (P9)

label: Italian Renaissance Fresco
defn: The fresco cycles painted on the walls and vaults of Italian chapels, churches and palaces from Giotto to the High Renaissance, studied where they stand: Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel, Brancacci Chapel, Sistine Chapel ceiling, Raphael Rooms.
see: A5-20 Italian Renaissance Painting;A5-16 Gothic Painting;L2-44 Gothic Wall Painting;L36 Illusionistic Ceiling Painting
note: ATTESTATION WEAK: no Wikipedia or Wikidata title for the cycle tradition; attested only through Wikipedia 'Fresco' (Italian Renaissance section) and the cycle articles (Scrovegni Chapel, Sistine Chapel ceiling); resolves the audit's tab-key-step-2 contradiction, but painters stay artist-led in A5 (P9) and the cycles are kinds — owner may prefer to make the cycles kinds of A5-20 instead

label: Generative Art
defn: Art made wholly or partly by an autonomous system — an algorithm, program or machine — from the plotter drawings of the 1960s computer-art pioneers to code-based generative work: Nees's Schotter, Molnár's (Dés)Ordres, Mohr's P-197, Casey Reas's Process works.
see: M2-2 New Media Art;L40 AI Art;A5-87 Concrete Art
note: remove 'generative art' and 'computer art' from the M2-2 aliases; 'Computer art' (Wikipedia) becomes the kind for the 1960s pioneers

label: Internet Art
defn: Art made for and distributed through the Internet from the mid-1990s (net.art), its browser, e-mail and website works and the post-internet generation: Lialina's My Boyfriend Came Back from the War, JODI's wwwwwwwww.jodi.org, Ćosić's ASCII History of Moving Images.
see: M2-2 New Media Art;M1-4 Mail Art
note: 'Net art' redirects to Internet art; remove 'Internet art' from the M2-2 aliases; post-internet is a kind

label: AI Art
defn: Art made with machine-learning and other AI systems, from Harold Cohen's AARON (1973) to GAN and diffusion-model works: Cohen's AARON drawings, Klingemann's Memories of Passersby I, Anadol's Unsupervised, Ridler's Mosaic Virus.
see: L38 Generative Art;M2-2 New Media Art
note: 'Artificial intelligence art' redirects to AI art; remove 'AI art' from the M2-2 aliases
